items.prompt: Ward Cunningham's original 'technical debt' metaphor compares a shortcut to what?
choices: A moral failing by the engineer who wrote it
A loan — principal to repay, interest paid while it's outstanding
A permanent, unfixable property of the codebase
A synonym for any code a reviewer dislikes
items.explanation: Cunningham's point was explicitly financial: borrowing (shipping the quick version) is a normal, sometimes correct choice, as long as you know you borrowed and intend to pay it back before interest costs more than the loan was worth.
items.reference:
🏦 Principal — cost of building it properly, whenever it's paid
🔁 Interest — recurring extra cost every cycle it stays unpaid
📈 Interest rate — how fast that cost grows or compounds

Why: Technical debt is Ward Cunningham's deliberate financial metaphor, not a synonym for messy code — it only makes sense once you can name what's being borrowed and what it costs to carry.
items.learnMore:
Loan termTechnical debt equivalent
PrincipalCost of the proper version, paid whenever you retrofit it
InterestRecurring friction cost paid every cycle the shortcut stays
Interest rateHow fast that friction grows or compounds over time
DefaultDebt never repaid, interest keeps compounding, velocity collapses

Why: The loan metaphor works because every term maps onto something concrete in the codebase — treating debt as a moral failing skips past all of it.

items.prompt: Nadia knowingly hardcodes a single-tenant assumption because of a real deadline. This is an example of which kind of debt?
choices: Inadvertent
Deliberate
Neither — it's not debt at all
Both, depending on the day
items.explanation: Deliberate debt is chosen on purpose, with the trade-off actually weighed — Nadia knows exactly what she's skipping and why, which is what makes it deliberate rather than accidental.
items.reference:
🧭 Deliberate — chosen on purpose, with the trade-off weighed
🎲 Inadvertent — just how it turned out, nobody chose it knowingly

Why: Whether debt was chosen on purpose is one of two independent axes (the other is prudent vs. reckless) — the same-looking code can land in different quadrants depending on how it was arrived at.

items.prompt: An engineer copy-pastes validation logic in three places instead of extracting a shared function, with no deadline pressure and no benefit gained. Is this technical debt?
choices: Yes — any messy code counts as debt
No — nothing was gained by doing it this way, so there's no loan to point to
Yes, as long as it's written down somewhere
It depends only on how many places it was copied
items.explanation: Debt implies a trade — something was gained (speed, a deadline, a market window) in exchange for the shortcut. If nothing was gained and no real pressure forced it, it's not a loan, it's just work done carelessly.
items.reference:
💰 Real debt — bought something — speed, a market window, information
🗑️ Just bad code — gained nothing, cut a corner under no real pressure

Why: Calling every messy shortcut 'debt' borrows the metaphor's excuse without its obligation — real debt requires a benefit on the other side of the trade.

items.prompt: Which of these is the strongest case for deliberately taking on technical debt?
choices: The proper version would take slightly longer to write
A real contractual deadline is three weeks out and the feature might not be needed again if the deal falls through
The engineer personally prefers to move fast
The codebase already has some debt, so a little more doesn't matter
items.explanation: A real, external constraint (a signed deadline) combined with genuine uncertainty about whether the investment will even pay off (the deal might not close) is exactly the situation borrowing exists for — spend less now, keep the option to invest properly once the uncertainty resolves.
items.reference:
✅ Reasonable to borrow — real deadline, market window, or an experiment that might get thrown away
🚫 Not a real trade-off — cutting a corner with no plan, no deadline, and no intention to repay

Why: Debt is acceptable when there's a real constraint forcing the trade and a plan to repay it — not simply whenever a shortcut is available.

Why: The presence of a real constraint is what makes borrowing rational — without one, 'just do it properly' was always the available, cheaper option.

items.prompt: Why does technical debt need to be written down somewhere shared, rather than just remembered by the engineer who took it on?
choices: It doesn't — remembering is just as reliable
Because a shortcut that lives only in one person's memory has no mechanism forcing it to ever get revisited or repaid
Because writing it down makes the code run faster
Because it's required by most programming languages
items.explanation: Tribal memory disappears the moment that person is on vacation, changes teams, or simply forgets — a shared, written record is what gives a shortcut any chance of being repaid on purpose instead of by accident.

🧠 Tribal memory — lives only in one person's head — repaid only by accident, if at all

Why: A shortcut that's never made visible has no mechanism forcing anyone to revisit it — it gets repaid only by chance, not on purpose.

items.prompt: A shortcut's principal is $9,000 and its interest is $1,200 per sprint. Roughly when does carrying the debt start costing more than fixing it up front?
choices: Sprint 1
Around sprint 7–8 (9000 ÷ 1200 = 7.5)
Never, since principal is always bigger
Only once the deadline is reached
items.explanation: Break-even is principal divided by interest per sprint — 9000 / 1200 = 7.5. Past that point, cumulative interest paid exceeds what the proper fix would have cost, so carrying the debt is now the more expensive option.

⏳ Past it — carrying the debt now costs more than fixing it did

Why: Sizing a shortcut means comparing projected interest by the planned repayment date, not just today's interest against today's principal.
